analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that federal highway and transit projects pay construction workers the local prevailing wage.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal prevailing-wage pay on federal highway and transit projects died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires that workers building highways and transit projects paid for with federal money be paid the locally prevailing wage — the rate typical for their trade in that area. This bill would repeal that requirement, letting contractors pay whatever they choose on those projects. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat in subcommittee until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, highway and transit construction contractors would have gained the most: they could bid federally funded projects using lower-paid labor, cutting one of their largest costs. Developers and firms positioned to win more bids at cheaper labor rates would also benefit. Supporters argued taxpayers would benefit if savings flowed into lower bids and more miles of road per dollar, but nothing in the bill required those savings to reach the public.

how_it_helps.text: By repealing the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement for federal-aid highway and transit construction, the bill would remove the rule that contractors pay the locally prevailing wage, allowing them to bid projects with cheaper labor.

Sponsors could argue this would stretch federal highway dollars further, since contractors facing lower labor costs could submit lower bids for the same work, though the bill text contains no estimate of savings and no finding to this effect.

analysis.who_pays: Laborers and mechanics working on federal-aid highway and transit construction projects would have borne the cost, since contractors would no longer be required to pay the locally prevailing wage for their trade. Nonunion workers, who rely most on the prevailing-wage floor, would have seen the largest pay cuts. Communities would also risk lower-quality work if contractors cut wages by hiring less-skilled crews.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the prevailing wage requirement would cut the pay of laborers and mechanics on federally funded highway and transit projects, reducing wages for construction workers in every state that uses these funds.

The bill's cost savings are speculative: if federal prevailing-wage rules are redundant with state laws or union rates, the savings could be small, while a wage cut for workers would be certain. The bill contains no offsetting protection for affected workers, such as training or benefit requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — more miles of road per federal dollar — rests entirely on the assumption that contractors pass their labor savings into lower bids rather than keeping them as profit, and it comes directly out of the take-home pay of the workers who build the projects. The cost is concrete and falls on a specific group of workers; the benefit is speculative and diffuse. An honest weighing finds the trade unfavorable, which is why even the bill's six Republican sponsors could not move it out of committee in two years.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in subcommittee from the time it was referred in February 2013 until the Congress ended, never reaching a vote in either committee or on the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Virginia Foxx introduced the bill on February 14, 2013 to repeal the sections of federal law requiring locally prevailing wages on federal-aid highway and transit construction.
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Education and the Workforce Committees, which sent it to the Highways and Transit and Workforce Protections subcommittees.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015, so the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded highway and transit projects are better off, because they kept the legal guarantee of the locally prevailing wage that the bill would have removed. Contractors who wanted to bid projects with cheaper labor did not get that opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers, who kept prevailing-wage pay

for.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the prevailing wage requirement for federal-aid highway and transit construction.

for.name: Reps. Lynn Westmoreland, Jason Chaffetz, and Joseph Pitts
for.what_they_did: Joined Foxx as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup, sending it instead to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, where it sat for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for the portions under its jurisdiction and never acted, with the Workforce Protections Subcommittee holding it until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would let contractors on federal-aid projects hire labor below the locally prevailing wage, lowering their costs on every federally funded road and transit job.

Union workers often earn at or above the prevailing wage regardless, so the direct wage impact would fall more heavily on nonunion workers, but removing the wage floor weakens unions' ability to set labor standards on public projects overall.
States administer the federal-aid program and would face lower bids on paper, but would also take on more of the burden of policing wages and handling disputes over contractor labor practices.

The prevailing wage requirement is a labor standard, not a subsidy; the bill offers no offsetting protection or savings mechanism, so any public benefit depends entirely on contractors passing labor savings into lower bids rather than keeping them as profit.
